title: Pre-Budget 2025: What BMS asked the Finance Minister
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Labour codes, tax exemption, rural micro industries and scheme workers: BMS's suggestions before the Union Budget.
body:
Each year, before the Union Budget, the Finance Ministry meets representatives of trade unions, industry and other groups. BMS uses these consultations to put the workers' viewpoint on record. In January 2025, ahead of the Budget for 2025-26, it did so again, and the points it raised show clearly what the organisation considers the most pressing problems of working India.

## What a pre-budget consultation is

A Union Budget is the Government's annual statement of how much money it expects to raise and how it will spend it. Before it is finalised, the Finance Minister and officials invite groups to present suggestions. For a trade union, this is one of the few occasions in the year when workers' demands can be placed in front of the people who decide the numbers. A demand for a better pension or a higher honorarium is, in the end, a demand about money, and the Budget is where money is allotted.

According to a report in *Organiser*, BMS wrote to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman after a pre-budget meeting held on 6 January 2025, and the report was published on 7 January. The report names the Finance Minister as the recipient of the letter and says the meeting was part of the tripartite mechanism, with officials present. It does not name the other participants, so this post does not either.

## The main points of BMS's 2025 submission

The submission was wide-ranging. Grouped by theme, the points reported were these.

**Labour Codes and contract workers**

- Notify the Code on Wages, 2019 and the Code on Social Security, 2020, and remove what BMS calls anti-worker provisions in the other two codes before notifying their remaining provisions.
- Regularise contract workers, with the Government leading by example.

**Taxes, pay and pensions**

- Constitute the 8th Pay Commission without delay.
- Raise the income tax exemption threshold to Rs 10 lakh, and exempt pensioners from tax on pensions.
- Raise the minimum pension under EPS-95 from Rs 1,000 to Rs 5,000 as a first step, and later link it to the minimum wage and to a variable dearness allowance.
- Extend Ayushman Bharat cover to EPS pensioners and provide old-age pension to all.
- Restore the Old Pension Scheme in place of the NPS and the newer Unified Pension Scheme.
- Form a high-power committee, including unions, management and Government, to plan the revival of sick public sector undertakings.

**Scheme workers and the unorganised sector**

- Recognise ASHA, Anganwadi, NHM and mid-day meal workers as *workers* and raise their honorarium; BMS pointed out that the last hike was in 2018.
- Fund the welfare boards, such as those for beedi workers and contract labour, which used to be financed through a cess.
- Provide special packages for plantation, beedi, agriculture, fisheries and platform workers.
- Continue MGNREGA, with wages not below the minimum wage and a guarantee of at least 200 days of work for each family.

**Rural enterprise and employment**

- Give priority to rural micro and small industries under the Production Linked Incentive scheme.
- Offer cheaper credit to rural factories, especially agro-based ones.
- Hold single-window digital licensing camps for small businesses at district headquarters, and set up Enterprise Development Centres in every district.

**Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh**

- Raise central funding for Anganwadi workers, since BMS says the state share has not risen in 15 years and stands at Rs 600, and clear the dues of daily wagers.

## Why scheme workers feature so often

Scheme workers appear in nearly every BMS submission, and the reason is their legal position. Anganwadi workers are engaged under the Integrated Child Development Services and ASHAs under the National Health Mission. They are paid an honorarium or a set of incentives, not a wage, and in most States they are described as volunteers. A column in *Bar & Bench* puts the Anganwadi honorarium at Rs 4,500 a month and the ASHA fixed incentive at Rs 3,500 plus performance-linked payments, and estimates that around five million women work across the three groups, counting mid-day meal workers.

The courts have not spoken with one voice. In 2006 the Supreme Court held in *State of Karnataka v. Amirbi* that Anganwadi workers do not carry out a function of the State, a view used for years to deny them worker status. In 2022 the Court held that they are entitled to gratuity. This is why BMS's request that scheme workers be recognised as workers matters: recognition would bring minimum wages and social security as rights rather than as favours.

## An earlier submission, June 2024

BMS made a similar presentation in June 2024, ahead of the Budget of that year. As reported in *Organiser*, All India Organising Secretary B. Surendran asked the Finance Ministry to extend MGNREGA to 200 days for each family and to consider including agriculture and allied work in it. He also asked for faster filling of about 20 lakh vacancies in central government, a pension of 50 per cent of the last salary with dearness allowance under all schemes, a minimum monthly pension of Rs 5,000, extension of Ayushman Bharat to EPS-95 pensioners, and higher honorariums for scheme workers. The repetition from one submission to the next is deliberate: BMS treats these demands as unfinished business.

## The pension numbers

The pension demand is among the most concrete. BMS also pointed to a contribution gap: under EPS-95 the Government pays 1.16 per cent on a wage ceiling of Rs 15,000, whereas under the Coal Mines Pension Scheme the same percentage is calculated on only Rs 1,600. A later press report puts the number of EPS-95 pensioners at about 8.15 million in March 2025, of whom over half, 4.9 million, receive less than Rs 1,500 a month. Those figures give a sense of why a minimum pension fixed at Rs 1,000 remains a central grievance.

## What the Government did around the same time

A pre-budget meeting does not produce an instant answer, and it would be wrong to credit or blame any single submission for what followed. For readers who want the timeline: on 16 January 2025 the Union Cabinet approved the constitution of the 8th Pay Commission, which officials said would cover about 50 lakh central government employees and over 65 lakh pensioners. On 1 February 2025 the Budget announced that no income tax would be payable on income up to Rs 12 lakh under the new regime, and that gig workers would receive identity cards, registration on the e-Shram portal and health cover under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, a measure expected to benefit nearly one crore workers. Readers can compare these with the list above and judge for themselves which demands were met, partly met or left over.

## Why it matters

Budgets are where promises become money. Unions that attend the pre-budget meeting get a chance to ask for the money to follow the promise, whether that is for social security, employment or the wages of those who work for government schemes. For BMS, which describes its approach as dialogue combined with protest, the consultation is the dialogue part: a reasoned, documented request made directly to the Government. What remains is to watch whether the requests are reflected in allocations in the years that follow.
